summary: A modular cryogenic link comprising superconducting radiation shields, copper braids, and a WR90 waveguide connects two dilution refrigerators over 30 meters while maintaining millikelvin temperatures and enabling quantum communication between spatially separated superconducting qubits. The system achieves base temperatures below 50 mK along its entire length with a 6.5-day cooldown time, and detailed thermal modeling predicts extensions to 120 m using additional cooling units spaced at 15 m intervals.
motivation: Scaling superconducting quantum processors into distributed networks requires connecting cryogenic systems over meter-scale distances while preserving quantum coherence; microwave quantum communication channels operating in cryogenic environments offer high-fidelity, broadband entanglement distribution without the conversion losses and added noise that plague microwave-to-optical transduction approaches.
method: A hierarchical modular architecture (link modules, adapter modules, braid modules, and a central cooling unit) contains octagonal copper radiation shields at five temperature stages, minimizes radiative and conductive heat loads through multi-layer insulation ($\phi_\mathrm{rad} \approx 1$ W/m$^2$ on 50K shield), Bluestone support posts, and high-purity OFE copper with RRR $\approx 210$. Thermal modeling based on Stefan-Boltzmann radiation, Fourier heat conduction, and measured contact resistances ($R_\mathrm{contact} \propto T^{-2}$ below 10 K) guided design optimization.
result: The 30 m system reaches steady-state temperatures of 10–15 mK at the nodes and below 50 mK throughout the link, with 4K and 50K stages staying below 6 K and 80 K respectively; waveguide attenuation is $\alpha < 1$ dB/km (0.03 dB total loss over 30 m), and the system maintains stable operation for approximately 6 months before O-ring seals degrade; thermal extrapolations indicate 120 m links are feasible with cooling units every 15 m.
